analysis.one_liner: Ends the insurance industry's exemption from antitrust laws against price fixing and monopolization.
analysis.headline: The House Judiciary Committee approved the bill in October 1992, but it never received a House vote before that Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1945, a federal law called the McCarran-Ferguson Act has exempted the insurance business from most federal antitrust rules — the laws that make price fixing and monopolies illegal in other industries. This bill would remove that exemption for four specific practices: fixing prices, dividing up customers or territories with competitors, forcing customers to buy one insurance product to get another, and monopolizing. It would keep the exemption for insurers pooling historical claims data and doing actuarial work, and would phase in the change over two to four years, with longer phase-ins for small insurers.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who buys insurance — drivers, homeowners, renters, and businesses — would gain the protection of federal antitrust law if insurers fixed prices, carved up markets, or monopolized, conduct that in other industries can lead to lawsuits and penalties and lower prices. State regulators and antitrust enforcers would gain a new tool over insurance pricing.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would strip the antitrust exemption for insurers who fix prices, so rate agreements between competitors could be challenged under federal antitrust law the way they are in other industries.

It would also end the exemption for dividing up territories or customers with a competitor, for tying the sale of one insurance product to another, and for monopolizing or attempting to monopolize any part of the insurance business.

The bill preserves the exemption for sharing historical claims data, computing loss development factors, and actuarial services — the functions small insurers rely on to price policies accurately — as long as they do not restrain trade.

As reported by the committee, the bill would phase in the change: a two-year transition period for most insurers, four years for small insurers writing under $20 million in annual premiums, and a lasting exemption from the trend-factor rules for small insurers with less than a 2.5% market share, easing them into competition.

analysis.who_pays: Insurance companies would bear the cost: they could no longer lawfully agree on prices or share territories through industry rate-setting arrangements that are shielded from antitrust law today, and they would face antitrust suits and potential damages for the covered practices.

drawbacks.text: Insurers and their state regulators have long argued that pooling claims data and trend factors helps small companies price coverage accurately in volatile markets; the bill recognizes this by keeping those activities exempt, but critics could argue any movement toward federal antitrust oversight adds litigation costs that may ultimately be passed into premiums.

The bill leaves state regulation in place as the first line of oversight and only applies federal antitrust law where state law does not regulate or where the four covered practices occur, so its real-world effect depends on how aggressively enforcers pursue cases.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: it would make price fixing by insurers illegal under federal law, as it already is in nearly every other industry, which studies and enforcement in other markets suggest tends to lower prices for customers. The cost falls on insurers, not taxpayers. The bill's own carve-outs — for data pooling and multi-year transitions for smaller insurers — blunt the biggest good-faith objection, that shared statistics are essential to accurate pricing. The main weakness is that it does nothing about the broader state-based regulation of rates, so its practical effect on premiums would depend on enforcement.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee approved the bill in October 1992 and put it on the House calendar, but no floor vote ever happened before the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. Jack Brooks of Texas introduced the bill on January 3, 1991, together with Rep. Don Edwards of California, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee.
The subcommittee held hearings in June 1991 and forwarded the bill to the full committee, which ordered it reported in amended form in November 1991.
The committee reported the amended bill on October 6, 1992, and it was placed on the Union Calendar — the list of bills eligible for House floor action.
The bill sat on the calendar for the rest of the session and never received a House vote; when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, the bill died and all work on it lapsed.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insurance companies are better off: the McCarran-Ferguson antitrust exemption remains intact, so price fixing, market allocation, and tying in insurance remain shielded from federal antitrust law.

for.name: Rep. Jack Brooks
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-TX); sponsor and chair of the House Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and, as committee chair, oversaw its reporting out of the House Judiciary Committee in amended form.

for.name: Rep. Don Edwards
for.what_they_did: Joined Brooks in introducing the bill on January 3, 1991.

for.name: House Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Held subcommittee hearings, marked up the bill, and reported it to the House with amendments in October 1992.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had two Democratic sponsors and cleared a Democratic-controlled committee, but no floor vote was ever recorded, so the record shows no roll-call or opposition vote to gauge the party split.

industries.note: The bill would have stripped the McCarran-Ferguson antitrust exemption for price fixing, market allocation, tying, and monopolization — practices shielded from federal antitrust law since 1945 — directly affecting the premiums customers pay. It would have kept the exemption for shared claims data and actuarial work, which cushions the change, but the industry's core rate-setting arrangements would have become antitrust-exposed.
